desc:
Give each lowercase letter a value equal to its position in the alphabet: a = 1, b = 2, ..., z = 26. The numeric value of a string is the sum of the values of its letters.

Given a length n and a target k, return the lexicographically smallest string of length n whose numeric value is exactly k. A valid string always exists for the given inputs.

n = 3, k = 27  -> "aay"    (1 + 1 + 25)
n = 5, k = 73  -> "aaszz"  (1 + 1 + 19 + 26 + 26)
hints: To make a string small in dictionary order you want the leftmost letters to be as small as possible. What is the smallest letter you could ever put first?
Start from n letters a (value n). The leftover k - n has to be absorbed by raising some letters, and each letter can absorb at most 25 more.
Push the leftover into the rightmost positions: walk from the end, raise the current letter by min(25, leftover) and subtract that from the leftover until it reaches 0.
editorial: Lexicographic order is decided by the first position where two strings differ, so the first letter matters most, then the second, and so on. That means we want as many as as possible at the front and the large letters pushed to the back.

Begin with the string of n letters a, which has value n, so extra = k - n remains to be distributed. Going from the last position to the first, each letter can take up to 25 extra (turning a into z). Give it min(25, extra) and reduce extra. Because k ≤ 26n the extra is used up exactly.

Why is this optimal? Any position that is left as small as possible allows the remaining positions to the right to carry the weight, and the suffix always has enough capacity (25 per letter). A smaller letter at an earlier position is therefore never blocked. The loop runs once over the string, O(n).
